title: Terrace mom sues Alberta after son's in-custody death
article: A Terrace mother is suing the Alberta government for her son's suicide death in an Edmonton prison in 2021.
Lana Greene's son died at 23 years old in the Edmonton Remand Centre on Jan. 11, 2021, where he had been serving time for the previous four months.
Timothy James McConnell, known affectionately as TJ, was arrested on Sept. 3, 2020, on charges of shoplifting and theft under $5,000 at a paintball store in Edmonton.

At the time, hoping that criminal detention would be a turning point toward recovery in her son's battle with addiction, Greene refused to act as TJ's surety - a requirement often necessary for a judge to grant bail.

But what followed, according to the mother, was neglect for her son's medical needs and months of torment. While none of these accusations have been proven in court, Greene told the Terrace Standard she hopes to inspire meaningful reforms and ensure others facing similar challenges receive the support and resources they desperately need.
Growing up in Beaverlodge, Alta., TJ was a vibrant and joyful child who loved sports, especially hockey, skiing and golf, Greene recalled.
TJ suffered two concussions in Beaverlodge, one in junior high school and one in high school, after which Greene noticed a change in his behaviour.
"I didn't understand at all. I just saw a big change in him, and then he started doing drugs, and that was something he was never going to do," Greene said.
In their household, Greene said TJ had been very open about the dangers of drugs, even identifying other students who used them. The sudden shift left her bewildered and concerned.
"Drugs were being sold in schools, and many kids were experimenting," she recalled. "It was frightening as a parent to see how accessible these substances were."
In Beaverlodge, a town of 3,000 people, the news of TJ using drugs spread quickly.
"Everybody who loved him before, started to look at TJ in a different way, which bothered him," Greene said.
Greene started to look for programs designed to support youth with addiction issues, but her experience was disheartening.
In Alberta, the Protection of Children Abusing Drugs Act (PChAD) is a program designed to safeguard minors facing significant risks due to substance use.
Greene sought a court-issued protection order for TJ under the program and TJ was put in a Protective Safe House in Edmonton for 30 days.
"They detain them rather than helping them," Greene said.

"I don't know one parent who had a good experience with that program. The police literally came in my house and ripped him out of our house. I've watched him get hog-tied by police. Forcing people is not good. It should be dealt with \[with\] compassion and treated like a health crisis."
According to Greene, police intervention under the PChAd program only made things worse.
"It didn't feel like they understood the complexity of his situation," she said. "It all just blew up after that."
Desperate for change, Greene moved to Peace River in 2013, hoping that completing school in a different environment would help TJ.

However, when he suffered a third concussion in Peace River in 2013, Greene noticed significant changes in his mental health. Depression set in, altering TJ's personality from the happy, active kid she once knew.
In 2015, TJ was diagnosed with bipolar disorder, a mental illness characterized by sudden and unusual shifts in mood ranging from high highs to low lows.
When it appeared the move to Peace River wasn't working, Greene started to look for a city with "a slower pace of life and an outdoor lifestyle."

She settled on Terrace and moved in 2016. At that time, TJ went to stay with other family members in Saskatchewan and Yukon who wanted to help out by providing alternative environments. He joined his mother in Terrace in 2017.
Upon moving to Terrace, Greene said TJ found a job on the first day and started to get better.
"He was doing very well here," Greene said. "I thought we were over that hurdle, but then again, I was not understanding bipolar disorder. It doesn't just go away."
After eight months in Terrace, TJ returned to Alberta with his long-time girlfriend in January 2018.
In Edmonton and away from Greene, TJ once again fell into the trap of drugs.
Greene was desperate to get him help, and she said TJ was ready, too.
"He wanted help, but every time we reached out, we were told to wait," she recalled. "Months would go by without any progress, and during that time, his condition would worsen."
Despite TJ's willingness to get help, Greene said accessing timely and appropriate treatment was a constant challenge.
At one point, she flew to Edmonton where they both walked into a treatment centre and begged to get him admitted but were refused, she said.
TJ also tried on his own but wasn't able to get follow-up care.
"He went and put himself in detox four different times and there was never a bed in the treatment centre for him to get into."
Greene said she called from one end of the province to the other because she would have driven anywhere to get him the help he needed.
"None of them had a bed because he needed medical detox," she said.
Medical detox treatment is the withdrawal of toxins and addictive substances from the body under the direct supervision of medical professionals to ensure an effective start to the recovery process.
Because TJ had a bipolar disorder diagnosis, none of the treatment centres would take him, Greene said.
"The reason he did the drug was because of the mental health issues. \[Treatment centres\] can only treat the drug."
In September 2020, TJ was arrested on charges of shoplifting and theft under $5,000. TJ's lawyer called Greene to bail him out, but Greene declined.
"My approach to parenting was never to bail my kids out," Greene said.
She believed this would be a tough lesson for TJ and would get him straightened out. She now regrets the decision.
"He was vocally asking to see a psychologist in the remand centre, which I saw as a miracle because I had been trying to get him to ask for help for years," she said.
Greene expressed frustration at the contrasting treatment between seeking medical help and being incarcerated.

"I find it very interesting when you're accessing treatment, they deny you because it's medically unsafe. But once you're arrested, they don't care, it's medically unsafe and they let you lay there and suffer," she said.

TJ's experience in jail was marked by severe neglect of medical needs, according to Greene. When he applied to be moved to another area of the remand centre for safety, they put him in administrative segregation.
"He was locked in a room 23.5 hours a day, let out for 15 minutes, twice a day. That was how he was treated and not given any medicine."
Despite being surrounded by drugs all around him in prison, Greene said he managed to stay sober for four months.
"Why, when you're arrested, all of a sudden it doesn't matter that it's medically unsafe to detox that way and nobody cares?" Greene said.
"He's not Ted Bundy, these aren't murderers, these are our kids."
TJ wrote letters requesting to be put on Suboxone, a medication that treats opioid dependence, but he kept hearing back that he was on a waiting list.

"I am scared I am going to lose my life when I get outside, back around even more pressure to use. I've overdosed 16 times and I really want to leave this life behind," he wrote in a health services request in November 2020.

Still waiting for help, TJ wrote another letter on Jan 1, 2021, saying, "I'm sorry to bug, I know I am on a waiting list, but I've been here four months and soon I'll be back on the streets, surrounded by drugs and hopeless addicts... please let me start my Suboxone treatment. I won't abuse this privilege."
Greene alleges a direct connection between his treatment in custody and his death.
"There's a stack of paper where he's begging for his bipolar meds and for medicine to not crave \[drugs\] so that he could recover," she said.
On Jan. 5, 2021, just six days before his death, TJ received another letter stating he was still on the waiting list.
On Dec 22, 2022, Greene filed a lawsuit in Alberta Court of King's Bench, alleging wrongful death of TJ.

According to documents filed and obtained by Black Press Media, Greene is pursuing $235,839.76 in damages from the Government of Alberta, including bereavement claims and punitive damages, under the Fatal Accidents Act and other provisions, as filed in court.

Alberta Courts Services confirmed by telephone that the Crown filed a defence to Greene's civil statement of claim on May 26, 2023. According to Court Services, the last activity on the file was on Feb. 8, 2024 when the Court of King's Bench sought directions on videos submitted as evidence.
As of July 19, 2024, no further activity had been recorded and no court dates had been scheduled on the file.
Black Press Media requested comment from Alberta's Ministry of Mental Health and Addiction and Alberta's attorney general, but the ministries refused to comment directly on the lawsuit.
However, a statement from the health and addiction minister's office did comment generally on current policies.
"Since 2021, our government has done significant work to improve addiction treatment and other health services within correctional facilities," the statement read.

"Because of work we have done to expand the Virtual Opioid Dependency Program, people in corrections can immediately access OAT (opioid agonist therapy) medication if suffering from an opioid addiction. This medication is now also offered by arrest processing units, meaning those taken into custody will have an opportunity to start OAT before incarceration."
The statement also says therapeutic living units have been established in four correctional and remand centres, including the one in Edmonton.
"These are designated units that operate as a recovery community, providing addiction treatment over the course of someone's time in jail."
Following TJ's death, Greene decided to stay in Terrace, where she has found solace in a supportive community.
Grateful for the compassion and understanding she received during her darkest moments, she acknowledged the vital role of community support in her ongoing healing journey.
"I have found a community here that has helped me," she said.

On June 26, Greene organized a 'Support Don't Punish' event in Terrace that coincided with TJ's birthday, advocating for drug policies based on health and human rights. Around 50 people attended the event alongside Terrace Mayor Sean Bujtas and Skeena-Bulkley Valley MP Taylor Bachrach.

Greene is a part of Moms Stop the Harm, a network of Canadian families who have been affected by substance use-related harms and deaths. A friend introduced her to the group in 2019. Greene said the network helped her understand what TJ was going through.
"You can also become sick with your loved ones and TJ never wanted it to affect us," she said. "I thank God I found \[Moms Stop the Harm\] before \[losing TJ\]."
The network also helped her immensely to cope with the grief of losing her son, she added.
For Greene, advocacy has now become an integral part of her healing process and a tribute to TJ's memory.
"If it just reaches one more person and changes the way they view it or think about it, maybe there's hope."
